name: Nome Lackee reserve established by Superintendent Henley, 1854
citation: Administrative action of the California Superintendent of Indian Affairs (per Royce); no treaty or statute
promises: Royce records only that Superintendent Henley established a reserve called Nome Lackee for the Nome Lackee, Nome Cult, Nir-muck and others. No treaty, statute or written promise of permanence was found.
today: This record is a reserve set up by a federal official, not a cession and not a treaty. No court or Commission finding specific to it was found; the California Indians' statewide claims before the Indian Claims Commission ended in a compromise.

nationVoice.summary: The Band says its ancestors were forcibly removed from their homelands in 1854 to a reservation further west, later walked the Nome Cult Trail in 1863, and lost their rancheria to termination in 1959.

sources.title: Charles C. Royce, Indian Land Cessions in the United States (1899), schedule p. 794
sources.publisher: Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology, via Internet Archive

openQuestions: This is not a cession. Royce records a reserve established, so the map should not show it as land taken by treaty.
When and how Nome Lackee was given up and its land disposed of, possibly under the Act of April 8, 1864 limiting California reservations, was not traced.
The Nomlaki may have been party to one of the 18 unratified California treaties of 1851-52; that belongs in an extra- record.
treaties.json lists the Grindstone Rancheria and Round Valley Indian Tribes; the Paskenta Band of Nomlaki Indians also traces its history here and is not listed.

plain.promised: No treaty was made. A federal superintendent set up the Nome Lackee reserve in 1854 for the Nomlaki and neighbouring peoples.
plain.happened: No court, claims commission or government finding about this reserve was found. The Paskenta Band says its people were forcibly removed in 1854.
plain.today: How the reserve was closed has not been traced.
